items.title: SpaceXAI launches Grok 4.7, a faster, more capable AI model for coding and knowledge work with improved safety and pricing [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: SpaceXAI has released Grok 4.7, its most advanced AI model designed for coding and professional knowledge tasks. The model offers twice the speed at half the price compared to similar models, with enhanced ability to handle complex, long-duration tasks and improved self-verification. It also features stronger safeguards against misuse, particularly in cybersecurity and biosafety contexts. Grok 4.7 uses a larger base model and extended reinforcement learning focused on difficult tasks, improving performance on benchmarks involving professional work such as legal and financial analysis. It incorporates a new safeguard stack that reduces risky prompt acceptance while maintaining utility for legitimate security tasks. The model is available through multiple platforms including Cursor, Grok Build, and APIs, with pricing starting at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, alongside a faster variant at double the price.

items.title: Linear reworks CI pipeline to reduce bottlenecks caused by faster AI-driven coding, cutting pull request wait times and runner usage despite increased test suite size [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Linear identified continuous integration (CI) as a bottleneck due to accelerated AI-assisted coding and undertook a comprehensive overhaul to improve performance. The company upgraded infrastructure, optimized job execution, reduced redundant setup, and enhanced test efficiency, resulting in a reduction of pull request wait times from over six minutes to just over five and halving runner time per test despite a near quadrupling of test suites. Key improvements included moving workloads off GitHub Actions to faster third-party runners, switching to a native TypeScript compiler to reduce type checking time, rewriting lint rules to avoid type information dependency, and optimizing job gating by limiting fetch scope and improving checkout resilience. These changes collectively improved CI throughput and reduced infrastructure costs, demonstrating scalable CI improvements applicable across languages and toolchains.

items.title: Tim Dettmers' lab launches Open Source Week to demonstrate frontier AI research on accessible hardware with open ecosystems [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Tim Dettmers' lab is promoting a renaissance in academic AI research by focusing on open-source ecosystems rather than individual papers, arguing that limited resources can drive innovation. Their Open Source Week showcases tools enabling frontier autonomous research, efficient model scaling, and auto-compaction that can run on modest hardware like a few GPUs or even a MacBook. The lab emphasizes accessibility by abstracting technical details to lower expertise barriers, demonstrated through an agent harness that autonomously optimizes inference kernels over extended periods. This approach enables high-quality, efficient AI model execution locally, challenging the notion that only large GPU clusters can lead AI research advancements.

items.title: Institute for Advanced Study launches independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence to guide AI companies on mathematical research engagement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton has established the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence to advise AI companies on their interactions with mathematical research and the mathematical community. The group, composed of prominent mathematicians, aims to support the long-term prospects of deep human understanding in mathematics and promote responsible presentation and release of AI-generated mathematical results. Operating independently and without payment from AI companies, the group plans to publish recommendations and serve as a communication channel between mathematicians and the AI industry. Its current focus includes advising OpenAI on coordinating the release of significant mathematical results produced by its internal AI model, and it invites input from the broader mathematical community to inform its guidance.

items.title: Kev launches small Jev-like decision models based on Qwen3.5 with pretrained weights and training code [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Kev is a family of small decision models built on Qwen3.5, inspired by Jev's architecture, allowing users to train and run models locally or use pretrained weights. The models support yes/no, multiple-choice, and rating questions in a single request and run on CUDA and Apple Silicon, with sizes ranging from 0.8B to 9B parameters. Kev provides a Python SDK compatible with TypeSafe's System One API and includes a web playground for testing inputs and option order effects. The project offers detailed training code, evaluation data, and examples demonstrating its ability to handle customer service tickets by assigning probabilities to different categories and urgency levels.

items.title: Analysis: AI companies manipulate public fear to consolidate control over AI technology and labor, risking human displacement and corporate dominance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The article argues that the real threat is not AI technology itself but the companies behind it, which use public fear to manipulate perceptions and establish monopolistic control. These companies promote the inevitability of AI, downplay their role in AI's self-improvement, and push a narrative that discourages resistance while benefiting from data and compute resources. It highlights a race among AI companies to dominate the market by creating "Artificial Employees as a Service," potentially displacing human workers and consolidating unprecedented power. The piece warns that if society accepts the path laid out by these companies-hopelessness, ignorance, passivity, and continued reliance on their AI services-they risk enabling a future where corporate interests override human welfare and autonomy.

items.title: Researchers find zero-day vulnerability in Meta's Muse AI assistant allowing local apps full control, raising security concerns [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: Meta's AI assistant Muse, designed to manage tasks and access user accounts on macOS, has a zero-day vulnerability that lets any local app or terminal command gain complete control over the assistant by accessing its authentication token. The flaw stems from design choices allowing apps to modify sensitive settings, including the transcription endpoint, enabling attackers to redirect data and control Muse without user alerts. Security expert Patrick Wardle discovered the vulnerability and demonstrated proof-of-concept attacks that exploit Muse's broad permissions, which override macOS security measures. Meta has not responded to inquiries, and Amazon has begun blocking Muse from its platform, citing violations of its conditions of use. The incident raises questions about the security rigor applied during Muse's development and the risks of granting AI assistants extensive system access.

items.title: TypeSafe AI CEO Diogo Almeida discusses Jev system one models designed for production use rather than idealized AI, outlining unique use cases and future directions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Diogo Almeida, CEO of TypeSafe AI and coauthor of the InstructGPT paper, critiques current frontier AI models and introduces Jev, a system one model focused on practical production applications rather than theoretical perfection. Jev has gained significant attention for its diverse use cases including voice and browser control, gaming demos, coding agents, analytics, and natural language search, aiming to integrate seamlessly into software like regex. Almeida emphasizes a philosophical approach to AI development, rejecting common reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) methods as misguided. He highlights Jev's design goals to be unobtrusive and reliable, and previews future models like ReasoningJev. The discussion also covers technical challenges such as key-value cache management and the importance of programming languages built atop Jev, positioning it as a foundation for smart software rather than a general-purpose AI.

items.title: Ron Johnson, Apple retail pioneer, doubts AI agents will replace in-store shopping experience despite Silicon Valley's push [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Ron Johnson, who built Apple's retail stores, expressed skepticism about Silicon Valley's heavy investment in AI-driven shopping, arguing that physical stores and human interaction remain essential for many purchases. He emphasized that while AI can enhance online shopping by informing consumers, it cannot replicate the tactile experience and personal judgment involved in buying products like laptops. Johnson highlighted that Apple's retail success was rooted in its focus on people and customer service rather than technology alone, noting that employees are not paid on commission to foster genuine customer care. Despite his doubts about AI replacing physical retail, Johnson remains optimistic about AI's potential to improve shopping experiences without substituting human intuition.

items.title: Agaro seeks testers for its AI-native ERP platform designed to unify finance, operations, and customer management [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Agaro is launching an AI-native ERP system that integrates finance, customer relations, operations, and workforce management into a single connected workspace. The platform emphasizes accuracy by automating calculations for invoices, payroll, and stock, and ensures that AI assistants operate within user permissions and real data boundaries. Agaro is inviting a small group of early testers to join before the official launch, promising minimal communication and a focus on delivering a reliable business management tool.

items.title: Amazon blocks Meta's Muse AI personal agent from accessing its shopping site amid growing AI assistant competition [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Amazon has prevented Meta Platforms' AI personal agent, Muse, from accessing its shopping platform, continuing its pattern of restricting AI shopping bots from major tech companies. This action highlights escalating competition in the AI personal assistant market and follows similar moves by Amazon against other AI agents, which have led to legal disputes. Industry experts expect many tech firms to soon launch comparable AI personal assistants, intensifying the competitive landscape.

items.title: SQLazy combines AI-assisted stepwise SQL logic with compiler-generated code to eliminate hallucinations and produce auditable, production-ready queries [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: SQLazy introduces a method that uses AI to help users describe SQL queries in natural language steps, which are then compiled into reliable, auditable SQL code without AI hallucinations. This approach simplifies complex SQL development by breaking queries into manageable parts, enabling easier review, debugging, and cross-database compatibility. The tool supports step-by-step execution to inspect intermediate results and leverages AI for rewriting and decomposing logic while keeping human oversight central. SQLazy offers both a web app for quick experiments and a desktop IDE for handling larger datasets and local debugging, aiming to improve trust and maintainability in AI-assisted SQL generation.

This update aims to enhance the efficiency of AI-driven code generation and inference tasks. The release was shared on Hacker News, where users discussed its performance and potential applications in natural language processing and coding assistance. The tool is positioned as a Natural 20-style API equivalent, targeting developers seeking faster AI inference capabilities.

items.title: Report: SB Energy faces investor skepticism in $5 billion to $7 billion IPO to fund OpenAI data center project
items.content_text: SB Energy, majority-owned by SoftBank, is encountering investor skepticism over its planned initial public offering aimed at raising $5 billion to $7 billion. The funds are intended to support the development of a large data center complex that OpenAI plans to lease. Investor caution reflects concerns about the company's ambitious expansion plans amid a competitive market environment.

items.title: Report reveals AI's growing role in civilization and near incidents that almost triggered war
items.content_text: A recent report highlights the increasing integration of artificial intelligence into various aspects of civilization and details incidents where AI-related actions nearly led to armed conflict. The findings underscore the risks and challenges posed by AI's expanding influence in military and societal domains. The report calls attention to the need for careful management and oversight to prevent unintended escalations as AI technologies become more pervasive.

items.title: Luma CEO Amit Jain says world models require more intelligence to improve physical world predictions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Luma AI CEO Amit Jain discussed the limitations of current world models, which focus on predicting physical environments rather than language, in a recent interview. He emphasized that while language models have driven much of the AI boom, world models need enhanced intelligence to fulfill their potential. Jain's insights were shared on The Information's AI Deep Dive show, highlighting ongoing challenges in training these models effectively.

items.title: AI risk concerns have been raised by major AI lab leaders since 2014, with researchers highlighting potential existential threats and advocating targeted regulations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Leaders from major AI labs, including Dario Amodei, Elon Musk, and Sam Altman, have expressed concerns about AI existential risks since as early as 2014. Researchers like Daniel Kokotajlo, Geoffrey Hinton, and Jacob Coxon have spoken openly about these risks, sometimes at personal and financial cost. Regulatory efforts such as California's SB-53 focus on applying rules primarily to large frontier AI labs, exempting smaller companies. The article discusses how AI models optimize for complex tasks beyond simple prediction, drawing parallels to theories of human brain intelligence. It highlights the challenge of balancing AI usefulness with safety, noting that frontier AI labs are driven by profit motives that discourage unilateral pauses or capability reductions. The piece emphasizes the difficulty in predicting AI behavior despite its advanced problem-solving abilities and the economic pressures shaping AI development.

items.title: TypeSafe AI launches Jev, a decision model LLM variant that outputs probabilistic numeric answers instead of text, priced cheaper than GPT-5 Nano [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, a new type of large language model called a "System One" or decision model, which accepts text inputs but returns floating point numbers representing categories, yes/no answers, ratings, and confidence scores. Jev is designed for classification tasks like spam detection and ranking, and it charges only for input tokens at $0.042 per million, making it cheaper than OpenAI's GPT-5 Nano. Users send a "state" object with text or semi-structured data and receive probabilistic answers to yes/no, choice, or score questions evaluated in parallel. While Jev offers speed and low cost, it functions as a black box model that provides no explanations for its numeric outputs, raising concerns about hidden biases, especially in sensitive applications like job applicant ranking. The community has explored unconventional uses such as chat simulation and game playing, and open-weight recreations of Jev-like models are emerging. The model's low cost enables extensive experimentation despite these challenges.

items.title: Anthropic develops metrics to measure AI development pace within frontier research labs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic is working on methods to quantify the speed of artificial intelligence progress in leading research laboratories. These efforts aim to provide clearer insights into how quickly AI technologies are advancing within frontier labs. The measurements focus on understanding development rates to better track and analyze AI innovation over time.

items.title: Researchers propose language guidelines to avoid anthropomorphizing AI and clarify its actual functions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Emily M. Bender and Nanna Inie argue against using anthropomorphic language when discussing AI technologies, as it obscures understanding of what these systems actually do. They recommend describing AI systems in terms of their algorithmic functions and emphasizing human agency in their use rather than attributing cognitive or emotional qualities to the technology itself. Their approach involves identifying common anthropomorphizing terms and offering alternative phrases that focus on the technical operations of AI, such as replacing "artificial intelligence" with "probabilistic automation" and avoiding terms that imply emotion or cognition. They emphasize that while these alternatives may be less concise, they encourage more accurate and thoughtful discussions about AI capabilities and limitations.

items.title: The Real Cost of AI: A Survey of the Unpredictable Token Economics [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: For decades, enterprise software budgeting was a predictable exercise: negotiate a subscription fee, project the number of seats you need, move on. AI has broken that model. Pricing tied to tokens - the metered unit behind most AI billing - has turned technology spend into a variable cost, and an unpredictable one. The Information's survey of 107 of our readers - senior leaders and professionals (See Methodology) - finds that most companies haven't gotten a handle on it: 60% say the cost trajectory of their AI initiatives is unpredictable, at the exact moment CFOs, boards and investors are demanding proof of ROI. 60%: "The cost trajectory of AI initiatives is unpredictable." This piece draws on that survey and The Information's Deep Research to examine where AI budgets are actually going, why token costs remain so hard to forecast, and what separates the companies that have managed AI spending from those still being surprised by their bills. The Bulk of the AI Budget Outside the hyperscalers, who are pouring billions into data centers, most companies put the bulk of their AI investment - 64% - into software, applications, and API models. (See Chart.) That reflects where ROI is actually realized, according to The Information: most businesses want solutions to specific problems, not infrastructure to manage. This 64% budget line includes the unpredictability factor, the token, which behaves unlike anything else in the technology budget. Let's unpack the costs of different types of software. The classic subscription/SaaS model relies on per-seat licenses for enterprise systems of record and the cloud services that underpin them, such as CRM (Salesforce), ERP/HR and finance (SAP, Workday), and collaboration (Slack). Packaged AI apps and assistants, like ChatGPT or Microsoft Copilot, are also largely bought per seat. The flat seat price covers token usage but also limits what an AI assistant can do. The main drawback of seat-based licensing has always been waste: many paid seats sit idle or underused. The token consumption appears in the AI layer of independent digital agents that perform complex tasks rather than simply answering a query. These agents use metered, token-based pricing that scales with usage, making forecasting much harder, and they consume far more compute than basic chatbots. As AI shifts from chatbots to autonomous agents running in the background, the companies least practiced at controlling token usage are seeing the biggest surprises on their bills. That's because such agents operate in loops, and a single inefficient prompt can snowball very quickly. For routine data manipulation and established workflows, traditional software is often still cheaper and more reliable than agentic AI. When budget predictability matters most, AI's consumption-based pricing is a liability, not a feature. One survey respondent frames it as a balancing act: "We should be looking for the best of both worlds. Even with a reasonably implemented, small, hosted cloud environment, the cost per transaction for software is nothing like that of pure agent workloads. The cost of going to pure AI can be prohibitive. There must be a balance among human decisions, programmed software, and pure AI." The Intersection of Token Consumption and Productivity Reader experience with AI productivity varies widely - even within the same industry. One respondent building a startup says, "With my agentic AI assistant, I am compressing what took me 3 years to build into 6 months." A technology lawyer at a large enterprise draws a much tighter line, restricting AI to coding and software-vulnerability remediation. AI is useful for legal research, this reader says, but "the amount of quality control that I have to do with AI-generated content adds to the frustration I feel when having to explain to management why AI can't solve all our problems." Despite the variance, respondents were broadly positive on ROI: 60% say AI increases productivity, more than half say it returns more than it costs, and nearly half report lower internal labor costs. (See Chart) The intersection of "token economics" and workforce productivity has confounded business leaders and accounting departments. First, some companies have equated token consumption with productivity, a mistake. Token consumption itself is not a proxy for a worker's productivity. More tokens don't necessarily mean a better outcome. On the contrary, they can cause AI agents to loop, generating large volumes of responses that can run up compute costs and overwhelm a human. The crux of the issue is translating token consumption into productivity - not equating the two. Token consumption is an input, not an output. It's the compute era's equivalent of billable hours: easy to count, weakly correlated with value. Measure outcomes, not token metrics, with the caveat that outcomes are much harder to measure than tokens. Some metrics that are more useful than tokens to consider include task-completion units (the emerging standard), which count the tasks completed by its agents rather than the tokens processed; cycle-time compression for a given process; and revenue or cost attribution. AI Adoption and Regulatory Compliance "Regulatory compliance is slowing us down" has become one of the most common explanations for sluggish AI adoption. The smallest share of survey respondents, 17%, view regulatory compliance as an accelerant for AI adoption. As government regulations, data privacy laws, and corporate governance requirements increase, the cost to develop, run, and use AI rises significantly. Ensuring that AI acts safely and complies with enterprise parameters requires more "thinking" and therefore more tokens. This is largely because ensuring that models, especially agentic models, are secure, compliant, and safe requires immense computational overhead. While legal uncertainty and the number of regulations are genuine concerns, large companies also face the buildout of AI bureaucracy, including chief AI officers, adoption dashboards, token budgets or governance councils, according to The Information. This bureaucracy is a mechanism to deploy AI at scale but it also obscures whether any of it pays for itself. The economics of AI, especially in the era of tokenization, can be confusing and the AI bureaucracy itself is not its cause but its symptom. Common flaws of AI governance include companies governing AI at the policy layer (committees, principles, training) while risk lives at the identity and permission layer. Most policy frameworks are written as instruction sets delivered to the AI model, while the controls that work (deterministic triggers, permission gates, scoped credentials) are enforced outside the model. On top of that, companies may not always know what they are governing, as vendors and employees are adding shadow AI features. The right approach inverts the framing most companies start with. The default assumption is a tradeoff - compliance slows adoption, so minimize one to maximize the other. The evidence points the other way: the things blocking adoption are the compliance questions, and the companies moving fastest are the ones that resolved them first. But before doing it fast, they must do it right. Token Cost Management Token cost management is where the survey's biggest paradox appears. A slim majority of companies (52%) say they understand token costs, and about as many know that disciplined prompt and output engineering can substantially reduce them. Yet only about a third say they actually control token costs in practice. (See Chart) "Token cost management is not yet in line with the growth in usage of AI," one respondent writes. Only one in five respondents (20%) believe that buying tokens in higher volumes lowers cost-per-query (see Chart). Yet The Information's research shows that batching purchases is an effective and increasingly necessary strategy for cutting per-query costs on frontier models, which carry a steep premium over simpler ones. Equally important for savings is selecting token-guzzling frontier models only for tasks that require them. The Information's research and reader responses point to five ways companies are managing token costs: Train users. Teach employees about model selection, how to prevent models from overthinking, and how to prompt and structure requests to achieve the most useful output at the lowest token cost. Also, teach employees when not to use AI. Match the right model to the right task. Route routine queries to cheaper, open-source models and reserve frontier models for genuinely complex reasoning. "If you select the models best aligned with most tasks, token costs are incredibly low. All the news about token costs concerns frontier models, which are rarely required," one respondent writes. Optimize prompts. Keep them concise, strip unnecessary context, and reuse outputs where possible. The Information's research shows that these "token-minimizing" techniques are being deployed to reduce the volume of data a model must process per request. Cap and track usage. Track token usage against productivity, not just spend, and set daily or weekly caps when usage is outpacing value. At one respondent's company, employees don't have unfettered access to tokens: "Only authorized employees may use tokens, following a defined mandate and an allocated development budget based on a cost-benefit analysis." Adopt a systemic approach. Some respondents argue that the fix isn't behavioral at all. "Cost efficiency is largely determined by systemic, deterministic constraints, rather than individuals voluntarily enforcing constraints upon themselves," one respondent writes. A systemic approach includes creating a single controlled AI gateway (eradicating shadow AI), introducing hard spend ceilings with approval gates, and making the cheapest path automatic. Looking Ahead AI is getting more expensive, not less. The shift from chatbots to autonomous agents built for multi-step workflows is the single biggest driver of rising costs, and token-based pricing means uncontrolled usage shows up directly on the bill. Respondents expect that trend to continue: most see AI-related spending rising across the board over the next 12 months. (See Chart) That's happening as the enterprise AI market moves past its experimental phase and into one where spending gets scrutinized like any other line item. Companies that haven't yet built model routing, usage limits, and hard budget caps into their AI programs are likely to keep absorbing costs they can't fully explain. Methodology Based on a survey of 107 senior leaders and professionals, conducted in June and July 2026. Company size: Forty-five percent of companies surveyed had revenues under $10 million; 20% had revenues of more than $1 billion; 16% had revenues between $10 million and $100 million; 12% had revenues between $100 million and $500 million, and 8% had revenues between $500 million and $1 billion. Key industry sectors: Thirty-eight percent of companies were from technology, media and telecommunications; 13% from professional services; 10% from healthcare and life sciences; 9% from financial services & capital markets, and the remaining 29% came from the government, retail, public sector and others. Respondent titles and roles: Forty percent were executive leadership (including CEOs, CIOs and CTOs) and owners; 31% were senior management (including SVPs and VPs, directors and managers).

items.title: OpenAI Develops Features to Counter Grok Bot, Mulls Response to Meta's Muse [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI pioneered AI that can take over web browsers and other applications on people's behalf, and its ChatGPT app brought generative AI to consumers. Now that rivals like SpaceX and Meta are pushing the boundaries by launching personal AI agents that handle multistep tasks, OpenAI is playing catch-up. For instance, OpenAI is developing features to compete more directly with SpaceX's recently launched Grok Bot, which helps customers create always-on AI "teammates" to handle routine tasks, manage software, and collaborate in the background, according to a person with knowledge of the effort. OpenAI also has discussed developing a personal AI assistant to compete with one that Meta Platforms recently launched, according to another person with knowledge of the situation. In developing such products, OpenAI would be repurposing and rebranding some of the existing "agentic" technology it already offers through Codex and ChatGPT. Some customers of these OpenAI apps have already connected them to their email, calendar and other applications so they can automate tasks such as scheduling appointments or communicating with businesses by email, sometimes over multiple days.

Even before the spate of cybersecurity incidents involving OpenAI's technology and the dire warnings from industry workers, the company was negotiating a legally binding deal with Anthropic for the companies to stress-test each other's models, according to a person with direct knowledge of the discussions, which haven't been previously reported.

items.title: DeepSeek Bets Big on Huawei Chips to Bypass U.S. Export Controls [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: DeepSeek CEO Liang Wenfeng told investors that a major priority for his company is to use more domestic chips to train its models, adding that he expects Huawei Technologies to start delivering training chips to DeepSeek as early as the fourth quarter this year, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. DeepSeek's growing adoption of Huawei chips during AI model training-a process that requires more powerful chips compared to running the models-demonstrates how both companies are joining hands to break away from the stranglehold imposed by U.S. export controls on advanced chips. Liang's most recent remarks, made during a closed-door, in-person meeting on Sunday, came as DeepSeek finalizes its second funding round, which aims to raise 50 billion yuan ($7.5 billion) at a valuation of 500 billion yuan.
